George Lakoff. An American linguist and cognitive scientist who pioneered cognitive linguistics by arguing that language structure reflects the embodied human mind and conceptual system. He proposed that human thought is fundamentally metaphorical—we understand abstract domains like time, emotion, and ethics by mapping them onto concrete, embodied experiences. He demonstrated that metaphor is not merely a literary device but a core cognitive mechanism shaping how we think and reason in everyday language. This insight challenged the Chomskyan view that syntax is autonomous from meaning. Lakoff argued instead that grammar reflects underlying conceptual organisation. He applied these cognitive linguistic insights to political language and rhetoric, showing how metaphorical framing shapes political perception and ideology. His work bridges cognitive science, psychology, linguistics, and philosophy, positioning language as emerging from embodied interaction with the world rather than as an abstract formal system. In doing so, he helped establish cognitive linguistics as a field and offered an alternative to the generative grammar paradigm that had dominated the discipline since Noam Chomsky's revolutionary work.
